title: Declarative node capability catalog and health ledger
content:
Purpose

This is a working proposal for a declarative node capability catalog paired with a "health ledger" that together drive service discovery and routing decisions across regions and tiers. Goal is to centralize capability intent (what nodes claim they can run) and a compact, conservatively-updated health ledger (what nodes actually are healthy) so control plane routing policies can be simple, auditable, and resilient across partitions.

Problem we are solving

- Current inventory is ad-hoc: labels scattered, different naming conventions per region, and inconsistent health signals (some agents emit load-only, others emit full telemetry).
- Routing policies embed a lot of logic (per-model whitelists, capacity estimates) which is hard to reason about in multi-region failover and can lead to opaque fallbacks.
- No single source of truth for GPU compatibility: teams maintain spreadsheet mapping models -> quant/precision -> GPU families. Hard to make automatic routing decisions based on model requirements.

High-level design

1) Declarative capability catalog (DKC)
   - Each node (or node pool) maintains a small declarative manifest describing capability stamps (immutable-ish attributes) and dynamic capacity hints.
   - Capability stamps: gpu_flavor, driver_version, quant_profiles_supported, max_seq_len, memory_bytes, network_tier, isolation_tier (e.g., shared/dedicated), region, zone, rack_id (optional).
   - Example stamp (YAML-like canonical form used by catalog):

   ---
   id: node-az3-c-1024
   region: us-west-2
   zone: us-west-2b
   gpu_flavor: a10x-48gb
   driver_version: 535.101
   quant_profiles_supported: [fp16, int8-awq, int8-ptq]
   isolation_tier: shared
   compute_tier: burst
   max_seq_len: 8192
   memory_bytes: 128000000000
   labels: [low-latency, high-throughput]
   ---

   - The catalog is intentionally declarative: nodes assert capabilities; control plane validates compatibility via rules and then endorses entries (signed endorsement for trust).

2) Health ledger (HL)
   - A compact, append-only ledger of health stamps per node updated by region-level health aggregators. Not a full event store — ledger entries are small delta records (epoch, node_id, observed_state, leases).
   - Observed_state is one of: healthy, degraded, overloaded, draining, offline. Each change includes cause tags (e.g., mem-pressure, gpu-therm, kube-evict) and numeric hints (current_qps, avg_latency_ms, free_gpu_mem_bytes).
   - Ledger operates with multi-region reconciliation rules: regional aggregator writes local ledger entries; global index keeps last-known-canon per node but allows read-mostly queries to tolerate eventual consistency during failover.

3) Compatibility matrix service (CMS)
   - Cross-references model requirements (e.g., sharded kv cache, fp16 weights, awq int8) with gpu_flavor capabilities. Implemented as a small policy engine that can be queried by routing logic.

4) Routing decision flow
   - Route = select nodes matching declarative capability filters AND health ledger status in allowed states AND routing policies (latency/cost/secure).
   - Routing tier examples: 
     * latency-tier: prefer nodes in same region with low avg_latency_ms and low tail-latency signals
     * cost-tier: prefer nodes with quant_profile that reduces token cost (AWQ) or nodes in less expensive region
     * secure-tier: require isolation_tier: dedicated and kms_policy: true

   - Fallback semantics: when no nodes meet full criteria, progressively relax filters in deterministic order (e.g., allow region-cross, allow degraded states with throttles, allow lower-precision quant). The order is policy-configurable per model/service.

Control plane and consistency model

- Control plane stores the authoritative DKC entries (post-endorsement) and the global view of HL (last-canon per node). Regional aggregators maintain local append logs and periodically compact them into canonical writes to the global index.
- Strong consistency is required for enrollment/retirement (e.g., marking node as permanently retired) but not for health updates — health is eventual. Routing decisions are tolerant: they read local regional HL when serving regionally, and read global (stale ok) when doing cross-region routing.

Service discovery index patterns

- Two indexes: capability-index (static searchable fields) and health-index (time-windowed metrics/last-state). Service discovery queries join them at decision time.
- Support two access modes: fast-local (cached, used by agent proxies for low-latency routing) and canonical (control plane console and bulk queries).

Health signal design details

- Signals to standardize across agents: free_gpu_mem_bytes, gpu_util_percent, power_draw_w, avg_infer_latency_50/95/99, qps, error_rate, eviction_count
- Health score composite: computed at aggregator with weighted contributions and a simple hysteresis window to avoid flapping (e.g., 3s sampling, 30s smoothing).
- Lease TTL semantics: agents post leases with TTL; absence of renewal moves node toward offline via a sliding window of ledger states.

GPU types and quantization compatibility

- Define GPU family tags (e.g., ampere-80, hopper-80, instinct-200) and micro-features (tensor-core-generations, fp16-accel, int8-kernel-availability). CMS contains rules like:
  - model: llama-7b-awq
    requires: [fp16-accel OR int8-kernel-availability]
  - model: rlhf-chat-13b
    requires: [memory_bytes >= 40GB, fp16-accel]
- For novel quant formats (AWQ, GPTQ, NuQ), include a short test-suite that runs a tiny kernel to verify execution at enrollment time. Results get attached to node's capability stamp as 'quant_compat_tests: {awq: pass, gptq: fail}'.

Operational playbooks (short)

- Enrollment: node boots -> agent reads local hardware -> posts declarative stamp to regional aggregator -> runs quant compatibility smoke tests -> aggregator endorses and control plane accepts.
- Degraded handling: aggregator detects high error_rate -> writes ledger entry degraded+cause -> routing policy either throttles or routes away depending on model policy.
- Region failover: during region outage, global index exposes last-canon states; routing policy switches to cross-region cost-tier fallback after exponential backoff.

Audit and traceability

- All DKC endorsements and ledger writes are auditable (who/what made change, signature/hash). Useful for postmortems and compliance.
- Control plane exposes a per-request routing trace: capability_filter matched, health_snapshot used (timestamp), final node chosen, fallback steps if any.

Open questions / TODOs

- How big should the HL append rate be? Trade-offs between telemetry verbosity and index size. Propose sampling at 1s for high-change signals but compacting to 30s for global writes.
- Do we sign capability assertions at the hypervisor or at the agent? Signing at hypervisor is stronger but harder to implement in cloud VMs.
- Should we allow ephemeral capability overrides (e.g., node temporarily reports extra memory via cgroup tweak) and if so how to avoid trust issues?
- Failure scenarios to test: split-brain between two regional aggregators, slow drift of quant_compat test results after driver upgrade. Add these to chaos test matrix.

Notes / links

- Related: CONFLUENCE-1234 "Node fingerprinting & GPU profile spec" (baseline vocab)
- Linked PR: github.com/redwood-inference/cluster-inventory/pull/257 (proto defs for DKC)
- Slack threads: #plat-inventory, thread: "gpu-compat-test-strategy"

Next steps (short-term)

- Prototype: implement a minimal aggregator that accepts declarative stamps, runs a tiny quant_compat suite, writes to a simple append-compact ledger (2-week spike).
- Policy engine: add a query API for simple boolean compatibility checks (1 sprint).
- Run canary in us-west-2 with 100 nodes and 3 models to validate routing fallback behavior (2 sprints).
